title: Margin
headline: Helping people get back the habit of thinking things through, one question a day.
summary: We scroll, react and repost, but we rarely sit with a question long enough to put our own thoughts into words. Margin is a small daily practice for that: one question, a minute to think, and an answer you write by hand in a notebook. I designed and built it on my own. It went from an idea to a live product, with real people using it, in two weeks.

sections.title: At a glance: what Margin does

blocks.text: Every day, Margin asks you one question. You put your phone down and think about it for a minute. Then you write your answer in a notebook and take a photo of the page. The photo stays on your phone, and only you can see it. By Day 30, you can look back and see how your thinking has changed.

blocks.label: Margin playing through one day: today’s question, a minute counting down, “Now, write.”, a photo of the page, Gap closed, and the page arriving in This week
blocks.caption: One day with Margin: a question, a minute to think, a photo of your page

blocks.text: Everything below this point is how I got there.

For a while now, I’ve noticed that most of us, me included, are slowly losing the habit of thinking things through. You can see it in any comment section: quick reactions, borrowed opinions, very little that’s our own. It’s tempting to blame AI, and maybe that’s part of it. But I didn’t want to point fingers. I wanted to find a way to get better.
So I kept coming back to one question: what would it take to make thinking a daily habit again, for people who are busy, distracted and, honestly, not very patient?

The phone is where the distraction lives. A thinking app that keeps you on your phone would just be more of the problem. That left me with a strange brief: design an app whose whole job is to get you off it.
Before I designed a single screen, I wrote down the rules Margin would never break:

items: **It never thinks for you.** No AI answers, no suggestions, no grading.
**The thinking happens off the screen.** The phone opens the practice and closes it. The writing happens on paper.
**Private by default.** No accounts, no feed, no likes. Your pages never leave your phone.
**Small enough to do every day.** One question, one minute, one page.
**No guilt.** No scores, and no streaks to lose. If you miss a day, you just carry on.

blocks.label: Margin’s welcome note turning dark as it is read, signed by Eucharia, then Settings: the daily reminder switched on, and “Your notes stay on this phone. Nothing is uploaded.”
blocks.caption: The welcome note says Margin will never grade you; Settings says nothing is uploaded

blocks.text: **One question, a minute to think.** My first version asked for 30 minutes of thinking. That felt right for the deep practice I had in mind, but a habit has to start small. So I brought it down to one minute, and people can raise it to 15 in Settings as the practice grows on them.
**Pen and paper.** Writing by hand slows you down and takes you away from the screen. It’s the decision people question the most, and the one I’m most sure about.
**The photo.** A photo of the page turns a loose notebook into a record. It stays inside Margin, not in your camera roll, so your thinking stays yours.

blocks.label: Saving the page: Margin asks for the camera, the page settles into the corners, a blurry photo is retaken, then saved
blocks.caption: Saving the page: if it’s blurry, take it again

blocks.text: **Questions that grow with you.** I wrote 100 questions across five levels. They start light (“What’s a song you never get tired of?”) and go deeper over the weeks. Everyone gets them in the same order, so I could design how they build.
**“Gap closed.”** Every day ends with the same two words. They’re small, but they give the practice a finish line.

blocks.label: After saving the page: Gap closed, “Same time tomorrow?”, the reminder set to 7:45 PM, and the page in This week
blocks.caption: The end of each day

sections.title: Building it: a website that behaves like an app

blocks.text: As a product designer, I’d always handed my designs over to engineers. This time I built Margin myself, with AI coding tools, all the way from Figma to a working product.

I wasn’t ready to spend the time and money on an App Store launch, and most of the people I wanted to test with use iPhones. So Margin had to work as a website. The catch is that Margin depends on two things websites usually struggle with: daily reminders and the phone’s camera.
So I made the website behave like an app:

items: You add it to your Home Screen, and it opens full screen like any other app.
It sends daily reminders as web push notifications, from a small server I set up.
It uses the phone’s camera inside the app, tuned so handwriting comes out sharp.
It carries your progress over when you move from the browser to the Home Screen, so nobody loses their first day.

blocks.label: Adding Margin to the Home Screen on an iPhone: Safari’s menu, Share, Add to Home Screen, Add; then the Margin icon on the Home Screen opens the app full screen
blocks.caption: From browser to Home Screen

blocks.text: I tested Margin with 7 friends over a few days. Each day I gathered their feedback and improved the product.
**“It isn’t sticky.”** This one stung, but they were right. Day 1 didn’t give people a reason to come back on Day 2, so I made three changes:

items: The Day 1 question now gives you a small “huh” moment: “What’s something small you changed your mind about recently?”
After your first page, Margin tells you: “That’s page one of your notebook. In a month, you’ll look back and see how your thinking has changed.”
Every day now ends with a hint of tomorrow’s question: “Tomorrow’s question is about a song you never get tired of.”

blocks.caption: A reason to come back tomorrow

items.label: The first Gap closed: “See you tomorrow. Turn on a reminder in Settings so you don’t miss your next question.” and a See today’s note button
Gap closed now: a hint of tomorrow’s question, why a reminder helps, and Set a reminder first; once set, “We’ll remind you at 7:45 PM.”

blocks.text: **People skipped the intro.** Some testers tapped straight through the welcome note and never found out what Margin was for. So now the Practice screen opens with the purpose, every day: “Margin helps you get back the habit of thinking things through.”

**The reminder mattered more than the note.** My first “Gap closed” screen offered “See today’s note.” But a habit needs a nudge, and the reminder is what brings people back. So if you haven’t set one yet, the main button is now “Set a reminder”, with one line on why it helps.

**Small things that broke trust.** On one Android phone, photos came out blurry and the app froze when it was opened twice. I rebuilt the camera and made sure only one copy of Margin can run at a time. On iPhone, a tester lost their day after adding Margin to the Home Screen. That’s why progress now carries over.

sections.title: What I said no to, for now

blocks.text: Testers asked for an app lock, typing instead of handwriting, writing their own questions, and more reminders. They’re all reasonable requests. But my rule is simple: one request is a note, two or three is a pattern. Typing and custom questions also go against what Margin is. So for now, they’re parked, not ignored.

items: **Constraints push you to find a way.** No App Store meant rethinking what a website can do.
**Design for Day 1, not Day 30.** Margin’s value builds over weeks, but people decide whether to come back after one day.
**Every product needs a clear “why”.** Testers didn’t skip the intro because they didn’t care. They skipped it because nobody reads intros. The purpose has to live where people already are.
**Building changes how you design.** Owning the whole product, from Figma to the live site, made me think about edge cases I used to leave to engineers.

blocks.text: A “look back” moment around Day 30, to keep the promise the app makes on Day 1. After that, the iPhone and Android apps.
Margin is small on purpose: one question, one minute, one page. But if it helps a few people think a little more for themselves every day, that’s the gap closed.
